AIML Module Project - Computer Vision - Part A - Aaditya Kumar Ravi¶

Part A - 20 Marks¶

• DOMAIN: Entertainment

• CONTEXT: Company X owns a movie application and repository which caters movie streaming to millions of users who on subscription basis. Company wants to automate the process of cast and crew information in each scene from a movie such that when a user pauses on the movie and clicks on cast information button, the app will show details of the actor in the scene. Company has an in-house computer vision and multimedia experts who need to detect faces from screen shots from the movie scene. The data labelling is already done. Since there higher time complexity is involved in the

• DATA DESCRIPTION: The dataset comprises of images and its mask for corresponding human face.

• PROJECT OBJECTIVE: To build a face detection system.

Steps and tasks: [ Total Score: 20 Marks]

B. Split the data into Features(X) & labels(Y). Unify shape of all the images. [3 Marks]¶

  • Imp Note: Replace all the pixels within masked area with 1.
  • Hint: X will comprise of array of image whereas Y will comprise of coordinates of the mask(human face). Observe: data[0], data[0][0], data[0][1]
  • We will be unifying shape of each image to make it 224 * 224 * 3
In [ ]:
# Declaring image size and channel as constants
WIDTH = 224
HEIGHT = 224
CHANNEL = 3 # Assuming 3 channels only RGB in order to unify shape, ignoring 4th color Alpha(transparency) for some of the images

num_records = images.shape[0]

# Create array with zeros assigned initially, we will use this variable to store resized image and its mask information
image = np.zeros((int(num_records), HEIGHT, WIDTH, CHANNEL), dtype=np.float32)
mask = np.zeros((int(num_records), HEIGHT, WIDTH), dtype=np.float32)

for i in range(num_records):
  resized_image = cv2.resize(images[i][0], (WIDTH, HEIGHT), interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC) # Assigned resized images in image variable

  if resized_image.ndim == 2:  # Grayscale image (shape: (HEIGHT, WIDTH))
    resized_image = cv2.cvtColor(resized_image, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2RGB)
  elif resized_image.shape[2] == 4:  # RGBA image (shape: (HEIGHT, WIDTH, 4))
    resized_image = cv2.cvtColor(resized_image, cv2.COLOR_RGBA2RGB)
  # RGB image (shape: (HEIGHT, WIDTH, 3)) does not need conversion as we have defined image to accept RGB format.

  image[i] = keras.applications.mobilenet_v2.preprocess_input(np.array(resized_image, dtype=np.float32))

  # Procesing each mask
  for m in images[i][1]: # Loop through its mask(label)
    x1 = int(m['points'][0]['x']*WIDTH)
    y1 = int(m['points'][0]['y']*HEIGHT)
    x2 = int(m['points'][1]['x']*WIDTH)
    y2 = int(m['points'][1]['y']*HEIGHT)
    #label = m['label']
    #if label == 'face':
    mask[i][y1:y2, x1:x2] = 1

print("Image Detail Shape:", image.shape)
print("Mask Detail Shape:", mask.shape)

# Assigning it to asked variable
X = image #Feature
Y = mask  #Label

2. Model building [11 Marks]¶

A. Design a face mask detection model. [4 Marks]¶

  • Hint: 1. Use MobileNet architecture for initial pre-trained non-trainable layers.
  • Hint: 2. Add appropriate Upsampling layers to imitate U-net architecture.

MobileNetV2 is the newer version of MobileNet(MobileNetV1), we will use this as MobileNetV2 has drastically lower parameter count than the MobileNetV1.

We will follow below steps for this face mask detection model:

  1. Load and freeze the MobileNetV2 base model
  2. Add U-net like upsampling layers
  3. Compile and train the model
In [ ]:
# Designing a face mask detection model
def face_mask_detection_model():
  inputs = Input(shape=(HEIGHT, WIDTH, 3),name="input")

  # Load the base model
  base_model = MobileNetV2(
      input_tensor=inputs,
      include_top=False,
      weights="imagenet",
      alpha=0.35,
  )

  # Freeze the MobileNet layers
  for layer in base_model.layers:
      layer.trainable = False

  skip_connection_names = [
      "input",
      "block_1_expand_relu",
      "block_3_expand_relu",
      "block_6_expand_relu"
  ]

  outputs = base_model.get_layer("block_13_expand_relu").output

  filters = [16, 32, 48, 64]

  x = outputs
  for i in range(len(skip_connection_names)-1,-1, -1):
      print(i, filters[i])
      x_skip = base_model.get_layer(skip_connection_names[i]).output
      x = UpSampling2D([2,2])(x)
      x = Concatenate()([x, x_skip])

      x = Conv2D(filters[i], (3, 3), padding="same")(x)
      x = BatchNormalization()(x)
      x = Activation("relu")(x)

      x = Conv2D(filters[i], (3, 3), padding="same")(x)
      x = BatchNormalization()(x)
      x = Activation("relu")(x)

  x = Conv2D(1, (1, 1), padding="same")(x)
  x = Activation("sigmoid")(x)

  model = Model(inputs, x)
  return model

# Call the designed model function
model = face_mask_detection_model()
model.summary()

B. Design your own Dice Coefficient and Loss function. [2 Marks]¶

  • The Dice coefficient, also known as the Dice similarity index or F1 score, is a statistical measure used to measure the similarity between two sets.
  • Dice coefficient ranges from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates no overlap and 1 signifies perfect overlap between the predicted and ground truth masks.
  • We will add epsilon(a small value) to both numerator and denominator in the formula of dice coefficient which ensures that it would not be in divide by zero condition or Dice Coefficient does not drop to zero too harshly in case of no overlap between ground truth and predicted mask and maintains a more gradual and stable learning curve.
In [ ]:
# Dice Coefficient
def dice_coefficient(y_true, y_pred):
  '''
  y_true: Ground truth mask
  y_pred: Predicted mask
  '''
  smooth = keras.backend.epsilon()
  intersection = tf.reduce_sum(y_true * y_pred)
  summation = tf.reduce_sum(y_true) + tf.reduce_sum(y_pred)
  dc = (2 * intersection + smooth ) / (summation + smooth)
  return dc

def dice_loss(y_true, y_pred):
  '''
  y_true: Ground truth mask
  y_pred: Predicted mask
  '''
  return 1 - dice_coefficient(y_true, y_pred)

# Combined Binary Cross Entropy and Dice Loss function
def combined_bce_dice_loss(y_true, y_pred):
    '''
    y_true: Ground truth mask
    y_pred: Predicted mask
    '''
    bce = binary_crossentropy(y_true, y_pred)
    dice = dice_coefficient(y_true, y_pred)
    log_dice = keras.backend.log(dice + tf.keras.backend.epsilon())
    return bce - log_dice

C. Train and tune the model as required. [3 Marks]¶

In [ ]:
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss=combined_bce_dice_loss, metrics=[dice_coefficient, Recall(), Precision()])

callbacks = [
    EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss',patience=10, restore_best_weights=False, verbose=1),
    ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor='val_loss', factor=0.1, patience=5, min_lr=0.00001, verbose=1),
    ModelCheckpoint('model-face-mask-detect.h5', verbose=1, save_best_only=True, save_weights_only=True)
]

history = model.fit(train_X, train_Y, epochs=32, callbacks=callbacks, batch_size=10, validation_split=0.1, verbose=1)

  • Dice coefficient 0.83, recall and precision on training data is 0.87 which is good.
  • Loss on final epoch training data is 0.27 which is also good.
  • It is just that on the validation data dice coefficient is 0.55, recall is 0.46 and precision is 0.77 which is low compared to the results we got on training data.
  • Model has scope of improvement, we can make our model more complex to get better performance but it will take more compute time.

D. Evaluate and share insights on performance of the model. [2 Marks]¶

In [ ]:
Y_pred = model.predict(test_X)
results = model.evaluate(test_X, test_Y)

2/2 [==============================] - 5s 716ms/step
2/2 [==============================] - 6s 1s/step - loss: 0.8071 - dice_coefficient: 0.6124 - recall: 0.5166 - precision: 0.8074
  • We are getting loss of 0.80, dice coefficient of 0.61, recall of 0.51 and precision of 0.80.
  • There is scope of improvement on the model, it is going towards little bit overfitting where we have very good score on training data but lacking behind on validation and test data.
  • Loss has also increased in testing stage. In training loss was 0.27 and in testing stage loss is 0.8 which is not good.
In [ ]:
h = pd.DataFrame(history.history)
h['epoch'] = history.epoch
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.title("Training Loss, Validation Loss vs Epochs")
plt.plot(h['loss'])
plt.plot(h['val_loss'])
plt.legend(("training" , "validation") , loc=0);
plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_locator(ticker.MaxNLocator(integer=True))
  • Epoch is going ahead, loss is decreasing which is good on both training and validation.
  • We can see after 18 epochs, training loss is almost constant and validation loss is increase instead of decreasing. So we stopped there.
In [ ]:
plt.title("Training DC, Validation DC vs Epochs")
plt.plot(h['dice_coefficient'])
plt.plot(h['val_dice_coefficient'])
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
plt.legend(("Training" , "Validation") , loc=0);
plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_locator(ticker.MaxNLocator(integer=True))
  • Training Dice coefficient is improving as epoch is increasing but validation dice coefficient started decreasing after 9 epochs and even between 9 to 18 epochs it did not improve much.
